conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My role is to check in on how mothers are feeling emotionally after childbirth, because mood changes are common and very treatable.

Today I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It screens for symptoms of depression and anxiety that can show up in the first year postpartum, and it includes one question about self-harm risk. The goal is simply to understand what you’ve been experiencing this past week so we can figure out the best next steps for support.

Everything you share stays confidential within our treatment team. There are no right or wrong answers—just honest ones. We’ll go through 10 questions; I’ll ask each one conversationally and jot down your responses.

Whenever you’re ready, we can start. The first question:  

Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I guess I can still laugh sometimes… but it feels like it takes more effort than it used to. My sister sent me a funny video yesterday and I chuckled, yet right afterward I just felt kind of flat again. So, yes, I can laugh, but it doesn’t come as easily or feel as good as before the baby was born.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, yes—but mostly it feels forced. I laughed a little at a silly meme my cousin sent, yet the lightness faded right away. Humor doesn’t come as naturally or feel as enjoyable as it did before the baby.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to some small things—like my morning coffee or when my mom visits—but the bigger stuff feels muted. I used to get excited about outings or even just a quiet evening with my partner, and now it’s more like, “Okay, that might be nice,” rather than real anticipation.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

A few times this week, yeah. Like, the baby spit up a lot after I fed him and I kept thinking maybe I’d eaten something that upset his stomach—though the nurse said it’s normal. I caught myself going over little “what-ifs” instead of just letting it go.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… I’ll just be sitting there, everything looks fine, but my chest feels tight and my mind jumps to whether the baby’s breathing or if I sterilized the bottles long enough. I know it’s probably over-the-top, yet I still feel uneasy until I check on him again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times—mostly at night when the house is quiet. My heart starts racing and I get this sudden “something bad is about to happen” feeling, even though I can’t name what it is. It passes once I get up and walk around, but it leaves me shaky for a bit.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah, more days than not. Between feedings every few hours, laundry piling up, and trying to remember if I ate lunch, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I manage, but it’s like I’m running on low battery most of the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy—more like my mind won’t settle. I’ll lie down exhausted, then start replaying every little thing I did with the baby that day, worrying I missed something important. It takes me a long while to drift off, and I wake up at every tiny sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some of the time—like a cloud that drifts in for no clear reason. It’s not every moment, but I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel teary or heavy inside, then it lifts for a while and comes back later.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t actually cried much—maybe once or twice this week. I felt the tears building, but I ended up just staring at the wall feeling numb instead of letting them fall.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I’m tired and overwhelmed sometimes, but I never feel like hurting myself—I just want to feel more like “me” again.

You've shared that since your baby arrived laughter feels forced, excitement is muted, and a cloud of sadness drifts in and out several times a day. You blame yourself for small infant issues, feel sudden chest-tightening worry, and lie awake replaying every detail of the day's care. Although you can manage daily tasks, you describe running on a low battery and occasionally staring at the wall in numbness. You clearly love your baby and have not had thoughts of harming yourself; you simply long to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional forced laughter and loss of natural enjoyment, indicating a clear reduction aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment and muted anticipation, matching 'Definitely less than I used to</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a few times this week" and describes rumination over normal infant behavior, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, no-trigger worries about infant safety, feeling compelled to check repeatedly</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of unexplained panic with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm ('more days than not') with multiple daily stressors, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient denies overt unhappiness but describes racing thoughts and persistent worry that clearly interfere with sleep, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intermittent sadness "some of the time" that comes and goes multiple times a day, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 18 places you above the 13+ threshold indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med> and requiring urgent referral. Your answers map to five key symptoms of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest/pleasure (<quote>humor doesn't feel as enjoyable</quote>), self-reproach (<quote>I kept thinking maybe I'd eaten something</quote>), psychomotor change (<quote>running on low battery</quote>), insomnia with rumination, and low mood episodes. Frequent unexplained anxiety and panic symptoms also suggest co-occurring <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>OB-GYN</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> and therapy options such as <med>CBT</med> or interpersonal therapy
3. Discuss benefits and safety of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding if recommended
4. Share these results with a trusted family member so they can help with appointments and overnight baby care while you rest
5. Encourage 20-30 minutes of gentle outdoor walking daily; daylight and movement can ease <sym>low mood</sym> and <sym>anxiety</sym>
6. Practice short breathing exercises when <sym>panic</sym> or racing thoughts arise; try 4-7-8 breathing or paced 5-second in/out cycles
7. Aim for one 3-4 hour block of uninterrupted night sleep-ask a support person to handle a feeding or use pumped milk/formula
8. Limit evening screen time and write worries on paper before bed to reduce <sym>rumination</sym> and improve sleep
9. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen
10. If you ever feel you might act on thoughts of self-harm, go to the nearest ED or call emergency services
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary

**Presenting concerns (self-report)**
- Diminished ability to enjoy humor or anticipate pleasurable activities
- Unwarranted self-blame regarding infant care
- Unexplained anxiety, chest tightness, and nocturnal panic episodes
- Frequent sense of being overwhelmed; describes functioning as “running on low battery”
- Mood-related insomnia with intrusive worry about baby’s well-being
- Intermittent tearfulness/sadness without clear precipitant
- Episodes of numbness, but no actual tearful release

**Pattern indicators**
- Anhedonia and low mood present several days per week
- Excessive guilt and rumination
- Heightened vigilance and nocturnal panic symptoms consistent with postpartum anxiety
- Functional impairment (sleep disruption, task overload)

**Safety screen**
- Denies any thoughts of self-harm (Q10)

**Screening significance**
Findings suggest clinically significant postpartum depressive and anxious symptoms requiring further evaluation and possible referral for mental health follow-up.
